title: Nucleic Acids, Replication and DNA Repair — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Nucleic Acid Metabolism: Structure and Function lecture (M. E. Annani-Akollor)

questions.stem: Which bond joins the nitrogenous base to the pentose sugar in a nucleoside?
questions.why: A β-N-glycosidic bond connects the sugar anomeric carbon to N9 of a purine or N1 of a pyrimidine.

notes.A: A phosphodiester is the backbone linkage connecting two sugar residues through phosphate.
notes.B: A peptide bond is an amide linkage between the amino acids of a protein.
notes.C: A disulphide links two sulphur atoms and is not the base–sugar linkage.
notes.D: Phosphoanhydride bonds are found between phosphate groups in nucleotide triphosphates, rather than at the base–sugar junction.

questions.stem: Which atom of a purine base attaches to ribose in a normal nucleoside?
questions.why: In a canonical purine nucleoside, nitrogen 9 of the purine bonds to carbon 1′ of ribose. This is the beta-N-glycosidic linkage.

notes.A: Nitrogen 1 is the attachment atom in canonical pyrimidine nucleosides, rather than the purine attachment site.
notes.C: Carbon 2 can carry a substituent in a purine but does not form the usual N-glycosidic linkage.
notes.D: Carbon 5 is a ring carbon rather than the nitrogen forming the usual sugar attachment.
notes.E: Nitrogen 3 is part of the purine ring but is not the usual sugar attachment site.

questions.stem: Which bond links adjacent nucleotide residues in an ordinary DNA strand?
questions.why: A phosphate group forms ester bonds with the 3′ oxygen of one sugar and the 5′ oxygen of the next. This 3′–5′ phosphodiester gives the DNA backbone its polarity.

notes.A: Phosphoanhydride bonds connect phosphate groups in incoming dNTPs rather than adjacent sugar residues in DNA.
notes.B: Peptide bonds are amide linkages between amino acids, rather than between nucleotides.
notes.C: Disulphide cross-links join sulphur-containing groups. The DNA backbone uses sugar and phosphate.
notes.E: The glycosidic bond at carbon 1′ joins a base to a sugar within one nucleotide.

questions.stem: What distinguishes ribose from 2-deoxyribose at the second carbon of the sugar?
questions.why: Ribose has an OH group at carbon 2′. In 2-deoxyribose the corresponding group is hydrogen, leaving the five-carbon framework otherwise intact.

notes.B: Both sugars have a 3′ hydroxyl in the free sugar. The difference in oxygen content is at carbon 2′.
notes.C: Both sugar structures contain carbon 5′ as part of the same five-carbon skeleton.
notes.D: Ribose and deoxyribose are pentoses and differ by one oxygen atom rather than an extra carbon.
notes.E: Carbon 1′ is the anomeric carbon that joins a base in a nucleoside. It does not supply the relevant amide.

questions.stem: Which feature largely explains why RNA is more sensitive than DNA to alkaline hydrolysis?
questions.why: At alkaline pH the RNA 2′ hydroxyl can lose a proton and attack the adjacent backbone phosphate. DNA lacks that hydroxyl, so this route of chain cleavage is unavailable.

notes.A: RNA and DNA share the usual purine bases adenine and guanine. Their ring nitrogens do not explain this difference.
notes.B: RNA can form duplex regions, but backbone cleavage in alkali is enabled by its ribose chemistry.
notes.D: RNA contains backbone phosphates, which are the targets of intramolecular attack during hydrolysis.
notes.E: The susceptibility depends on the 2′ hydroxyl of ribose regardless of how many adenines are present.

questions.stem: Which strand orientation is characteristic of the Watson-Crick DNA double helix?
questions.why: The 5′ to 3′ direction of one DNA backbone runs opposite the 5′ to 3′ direction of the other. This antiparallel arrangement supports canonical complementary base pairing.

notes.A: Parallel strands would run in the same 5′ to 3′ direction, unlike the backbones of the Watson–Crick duplex.
notes.B: Strand orientation is constrained by the geometry of the base pairs rather than arranged randomly.
notes.C: The strands are associated by noncovalent interactions. Covalent phosphodiester links are within each strand.
notes.D: Both linear and circular DNA can have two antiparallel strands.

questions.stem: How many hydrogen bonds occur in a standard guanine-cytosine base pair?
questions.why: The donor and acceptor groups of guanine and cytosine align to form three hydrogen bonds in a standard Watson–Crick pair. Adenine and thymine form two.

notes.A: Two hydrogen bonds are characteristic of the standard adenine–thymine pair.
notes.C: One bond is insufficient to account for the three standard interactions between guanine and cytosine.
notes.D: Standard guanine and cytosine pairing has three aligned donor–acceptor interactions rather than four.
notes.E: Five bonds exceed the number supported by the standard guanine–cytosine pairing geometry.

questions.stem: Why does a GC-rich DNA duplex generally melt at a higher temperature than a comparable AT-rich duplex?

options.label: A
options.text: Fewer phosphate groups in its backbone

options.label: B
options.text: A different sugar in each strand

questions.why: At comparable lengths and solution conditions, GC-rich DNA usually has a higher melting temperature. Both base-pair interactions and the sequence-dependent stacking of neighbouring bases contribute to stability.

notes.A: Matching strand lengths give comparable numbers of backbone phosphate groups. Base composition primarily affects interactions among bases.
notes.B: The two strands both contain deoxyribose regardless of their GC content.
notes.C: Complementary bases are held together by noncovalent interactions rather than direct covalent bonds.
notes.E: No bound RNA is needed for GC-dependent variation in the stability of a DNA duplex.

questions.stem: What does the melting temperature of a DNA duplex represent?

options.label: C
options.text: All bases have been chemically removed

options.label: D
options.text: Half of phosphate bonds are cleaved

questions.why: Melting temperature is the midpoint of the thermal transition under specified conditions. For a simple two-state duplex, about half of the molecules are dissociated at that temperature.

notes.B: Thermal melting generally separates strands without fragmenting their covalent backbones.
notes.C: The bases remain attached to their sugars when the strands separate.
notes.D: Strand separation disrupts noncovalent interactions without cleaving half the phosphodiester bonds.
notes.E: The melting midpoint measures the duplex transition and is not a test of whether RNA is present.

questions.stem: What change in absorbance at 260 nm accompanies thermal DNA denaturation?

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in UV light absorbance

options.label: E
options.text: A loss of all purine absorption

questions.why: DNA bases absorb ultraviolet light near 260 nm. Strand separation disrupts base stacking, increasing their absorbance through the hyperchromic effect.

notes.A: Separated DNA strands retain ultraviolet-absorbing bases and therefore do not lose all absorbance.
notes.B: Loss of stacking changes the optical properties of the bases even though they remain chemically intact.
notes.D: The measured change occurs in the ultraviolet, at the same monitored wavelength near 260 nm.
notes.E: Purine bases still absorb ultraviolet light after separation, as do the pyrimidines.

questions.stem: Which type of DNA helix is the common physiological right-handed form?
questions.why: B-DNA is the usual right-handed double helix of hydrated DNA under physiological conditions. Its bases lie roughly perpendicular to the helical axis.

notes.A: A-DNA is also right-handed, but is favoured by reduced hydration rather than usual hydrated conditions.
notes.B: Z-DNA is a left-handed helix associated with some sequences and conditions.
notes.C: Cruciform DNA contains a cross-shaped secondary structure and is not the usual full-length duplex conformation.
notes.D: Triple-helical DNA has an additional strand associated with a duplex, rather than the standard two-stranded B form.

questions.stem: Which DNA conformation is notably left-handed rather than right-handed?
questions.why: In Z-DNA, the two strands wind into a left-handed helix with a zigzag backbone. The usual A and B forms instead have right-handed geometry.

notes.A: The B form is the ordinary right-handed helix of hydrated DNA.
notes.C: The A form of DNA is right-handed and is favoured at lower hydration.
notes.D: Standard double-stranded RNA adopts a right-handed A-form helix.
notes.E: Canonical B-DNA has right-handed geometry and does not have the zigzag conformation of Z-DNA.

questions.stem: Which DNA conformation is commonly favoured in dehydrating conditions and resembles the geometry of double-stranded RNA?
questions.why: Low hydration favours the right-handed A form of DNA, which has inclined base pairs and a shorter rise per base pair than B-DNA. RNA duplexes typically adopt A-like geometry.

notes.A: B-DNA is favoured under ordinary hydrated conditions and has a different base-pair orientation.
notes.B: Z-DNA is left-handed and is not the usual helix of double-stranded RNA.
notes.C: A nucleosome core is a DNA–histone assembly rather than a distinct conformation of free dehydrated DNA.
notes.E: A single-stranded coil lacks the regular two-strand geometry shared by A-DNA and typical RNA duplexes.

questions.stem: Which structural feature packages eukaryotic DNA into repeating chromatin units?

options.label: C
options.text: DNA in a free cytosolic circle

options.label: D
options.text: DNA bound solely to RNA polymerase

options.label: E
options.text: DNA enclosed in a membrane vesicle

questions.why: A nucleosome contains DNA wrapped around an octamer of core histones. Repeated nucleosomes organise and compact eukaryotic chromatin.

notes.B: Ribosomes translate messenger RNA and do not provide the repeating DNA-packaging units of eukaryotic chromatin.
notes.C: A free DNA circle does not describe the repeating DNA–protein units that package nuclear chromosomes.
notes.D: RNA polymerase uses DNA as a transcription template and is not the core protein of nucleosomes.
notes.E: Membrane vesicles do not form the repeating structural units of chromatin.

questions.stem: What is the main functional role of the histone H1 protein?
questions.why: Histone H1 binds near the entry and exit of DNA from a nucleosome and contacts linker DNA. This helps stabilise local packing and chromatin compaction.

notes.A: Translation occurs at ribosomes and does not require H1 as a catalyst.
notes.B: Helicases separate the templates at replication forks. H1 instead helps package DNA.
notes.D: The synthesis of ribose phosphate involves metabolic enzymes rather than linker histone.
notes.E: Nucleotide-excision repair removes UV-induced DNA lesions. H1 is not the enzyme that excises them.

questions.stem: Which RNA type directly carries amino acids to the ribosome?
questions.why: An aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase attaches an amino acid to its tRNA. The charged tRNA delivers that amino acid to the ribosome, matching its anticodon to the mRNA codon.

notes.A: Messenger RNA supplies the sequence of codons specifying the order of amino acids.
notes.B: Ribosomal RNA forms structural and catalytic parts of the ribosome rather than carrying individual amino acids.
notes.C: Small nuclear RNAs participate in RNA processing, including splicing, rather than bringing amino acids to ribosomes.
notes.D: Long noncoding RNAs can regulate gene activity but are not the standard amino acid adaptors in translation.

questions.stem: Which RNA type is a major structural and catalytic component of ribosomes?
questions.why: Ribosomal RNAs form much of the ribosome's core. In the large subunit, rRNA constitutes the active centre that catalyses peptide-bond formation.

notes.A: Messenger RNA provides the template that is read by the ribosome. It is not a structural catalyst within it.
notes.C: Transfer RNA brings amino acids to the ribosome and participates in decoding each codon.
notes.D: Small interfering RNA helps guide sequence-specific gene silencing rather than building the ribosome.
notes.E: MicroRNAs regulate gene expression by interacting with target transcripts and are not the ribosome's catalytic component.

questions.stem: Which tRNA sequence is the amino-acid attachment site near its mature 3-prime end?
questions.why: Mature tRNAs end in the conserved sequence CCA. The amino acid is esterified to the ribose of the terminal adenosine.

notes.A: TATA is associated with certain DNA promoters rather than the amino acid acceptor end of mature tRNA.
notes.B: AUG commonly acts as an mRNA start codon and is not the acceptor sequence.
notes.C: UAA is a stop codon read during translation, not the conserved tRNA acceptor end.
notes.E: A GGAG sequence can be related to bacterial ribosome-binding motifs, but does not form the tRNA acceptor end.

questions.stem: Which RNA sequence pairs with a complementary mRNA codon during translation?
questions.why: The three-base anticodon in tRNA pairs with the corresponding mRNA codon in the ribosome. This positions the attached amino acid according to the coded sequence.

notes.B: A promoter is a DNA region that affects transcription initiation rather than pairing with a codon during translation.
notes.C: A DNA enhancer regulates transcription and is not the nucleotide triplet that reads a codon.
notes.D: A transcription terminator governs RNA synthesis rather than recognition of a codon by charged tRNA.
notes.E: A histone tail is protein and participates in chromatin regulation, not complementary base pairing.

questions.stem: Why can DNA distinguish spontaneous cytosine deamination from normal base identity?

options.label: A
options.text: Cytosine is normally absent from DNA

options.label: B
options.text: Adenine is normally absent from DNA

options.label: C
options.text: Uracil is normally absent from DNA

options.label: D
options.text: Thymine is normally absent from DNA

options.label: E
options.text: Guanine is normally absent from DNA

questions.why: Spontaneous cytosine deamination produces uracil, which is not a standard DNA base. Uracil-DNA glycosylase can remove it, allowing base-excision repair to restore the correct nucleotide.

notes.A: Cytosine is a canonical DNA pyrimidine. Its conversion to an atypical residue is what creates the repair signal.
notes.B: Adenine is a normal DNA purine that pairs with thymine.
notes.D: Thymine is the canonical DNA partner of adenine, making an unmodified uracil residue unusual in DNA.
notes.E: Guanine is a canonical DNA purine and ordinarily pairs with cytosine.

questions.stem: What does semiconservative DNA replication produce from one parental duplex?

options.label: A
options.text: One duplex containing both old strands

options.label: B
options.text: Two duplexes with only newly made strands

options.label: C
options.text: Four duplexes with alternating base pairs

options.label: D
options.text: One duplex containing two new strands

options.label: E
options.text: Two duplexes each with one old strand

questions.why: The parental DNA strands separate and each directs synthesis of its complement. Each of the two daughter duplexes therefore contains one original strand and one new strand.

notes.A: Retention of both parental strands in the same daughter duplex would describe conservative replication.
notes.B: Newly synthesised strands pair with parental templates, so the products do not consist exclusively of new strands.
notes.C: Replication of one duplex produces two duplexes, each assembled from a parental template and its new complement.
notes.D: Each daughter duplex contains a parental template rather than being made of two new strands.

questions.stem: In which direction do DNA polymerases extend a newly synthesised DNA strand?

options.label: D
options.text: In both directions in one chain

questions.why: DNA polymerases add each dNTP to a free 3′ hydroxyl, extending the strand 5′→3′.

notes.A: Polymerase reads the template in the 3′ to 5′ direction but adds to the 3′ end of the growing strand.
notes.C: Two forks can diverge from an origin, but a single new strand still grows only by extension at its 3′ end.
notes.D: Opposite forks can move in different directions, while synthesis of each individual chain maintains the same polarity.
notes.E: The chemistry requires a free 3′ hydroxyl at the growing end and therefore specifies a direction.

questions.stem: Which molecular feature is required before a DNA polymerase can start chain elongation?

options.label: A
options.text: A free nucleotide with a 5-prime OH

options.label: D
options.text: An existing primer with a 3-prime OH

questions.why: A replicative DNA polymerase needs a pre-existing primer paired with a template. The primer's free 3′ hydroxyl attacks the incoming nucleotide to extend the chain.

notes.A: A 5′ hydroxyl is not the group extended in the polymerase reaction.
notes.B: Ribosomes translate mRNA rather than priming DNA chain synthesis.
notes.C: Histone methylation can influence chromatin, but the immediate chemical requirement is a primer with a free 3′ end.
notes.E: Membrane pores allow passage of molecules and are unrelated to the primer requirement.

questions.stem: Why is the leading DNA strand synthesized continuously at an advancing replication fork?

options.label: A
options.text: Its template permits extension toward the fork

options.label: D
options.text: Its strand contains no phosphate groups

options.label: E
options.text: Its polymerase does not need a primer

questions.why: The leading template runs 3′ to 5′ in the direction the fork advances. Polymerase can therefore extend the new strand continuously 5′ to 3′ towards the opening fork.

notes.B: The template must contain bases to specify complementary nucleotide incorporation.
notes.C: DNA polymerases extend new DNA 5′ to 3′ on both strands, irrespective of the fork direction.
notes.D: The leading strand, like the lagging strand, is built with a sugar–phosphate backbone.
notes.E: Leading-strand synthesis still requires an initial primer even though repeated priming is characteristic of the lagging strand.

questions.stem: What is the defining difference of lagging-strand DNA synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: DNA is synthesized entirely from RNA bases

options.label: B
options.text: No primer is needed for elongation

options.label: E
options.text: The strand lacks any covalent backbone

questions.why: The lagging template opens in an orientation opposite to the direction in which its daughter strand can grow. Polymerase therefore extends successive primers to make short Okazaki fragments.

notes.A: RNA can provide the initial primer, but most of the fragment consists of DNA made from deoxyribonucleotides.
notes.B: Each Okazaki fragment requires a new primer with a free 3′ hydroxyl for elongation.
notes.D: Polymerase follows the template 3′ to 5′ on either strand. Discontinuous synthesis is the distinguishing feature.
notes.E: Okazaki fragments have covalent backbones and are joined after primer removal and replacement.

questions.stem: Which enzyme generates the short RNA primers needed to initiate Okazaki fragments?
questions.why: DNA primase makes a short RNA strand complementary to the template. Its 3′ hydroxyl provides the end that replicative DNA polymerase extends.

notes.A: DNA ligase seals a nick between adjacent strands after synthesis and does not make the initial RNA primer.
notes.B: A type II topoisomerase alters DNA topology rather than making an RNA primer.
notes.C: Exonuclease III can degrade DNA from certain 3′ ends but cannot synthesise a primer for DNA polymerase.
notes.D: Telomerase extends chromosome ends using its own RNA template rather than priming internal Okazaki fragments.

questions.stem: Which enzyme seals remaining backbone nicks between fully processed Okazaki fragments?
questions.why: Once the RNA primer has been replaced, a nick can remain between an upstream 3′ hydroxyl and downstream 5′ phosphate. DNA ligase forms the missing phosphodiester bond.

notes.A: Helicase opens the parental duplex and does not covalently join neighbouring DNA segments.
notes.C: Primase synthesises RNA primers when a fragment begins, rather than sealing its final backbone nick.
notes.D: DNA gyrase is a bacterial topoisomerase that manages supercoiling rather than joining processed fragments.
notes.E: RNA polymerase II transcribes eukaryotic genes and does not seal DNA.

questions.stem: Which enzyme separates the two parental DNA strands at a replication fork?
questions.why: Replicative helicase uses ATP to separate the parental strands at a fork. This exposes the bases of each strand so that they can serve as templates.

notes.A: DNA ligase joins DNA ends after synthesis rather than separating duplex strands.
notes.B: A methylase modifies selected DNA bases and does not drive strand separation at the fork.
notes.C: DNA polymerase beta mainly fills short gaps during repair rather than opening parental DNA.
notes.E: Splicing factors participate in processing RNA transcripts, not in separating replication templates.

questions.stem: Why does DNA topoisomerase activity become essential as a replication fork advances?

options.label: A
options.text: Relief of torsional strain at the fork

options.label: B
options.text: It inserts amino acids into DNA strands

options.label: C
options.text: It translates a parental coding strand

options.label: D
options.text: It ligates the mRNA cap to a primer

questions.why: Opening the duplex at the fork can introduce positive supercoiling ahead of it. Topoisomerases transiently cleave and reseal DNA to relieve that torsional strain.

notes.B: Amino acids are incorporated into proteins by translation, rather than into replicating DNA.
notes.C: DNA replication copies a nucleotide template. Translation requires an mRNA and a ribosome.
notes.D: The mRNA cap is a transcript modification and is not attached to a replication primer by topoisomerases.
notes.E: Topoisomerases change DNA topology without replacing purines or pyrimidines.

questions.stem: Which bacterial enzyme introduces negative supercoils and relieves replication-associated torsion?
questions.why: DNA gyrase is a bacterial type II topoisomerase that can introduce negative supercoils. Its activity also counteracts the positive torsion that accumulates ahead of a replication fork.

notes.A: DNA ligase forms backbone bonds at nicks without performing the strand-passage reaction.
notes.B: Primase synthesises primers for replication but does not change DNA supercoiling.
notes.D: DNA polymerase I replaces RNA primers with DNA and does not introduce negative supercoils.
notes.E: A restriction enzyme is a sequence-specific nuclease and does not perform gyrase's controlled strand passage and resealing.

questions.stem: Which enzyme has the major bacterial replicative DNA synthesis activity?
questions.why: In the standard E. coli model, DNA polymerase III carries out most chromosomal DNA synthesis on both leading and lagging strands. Associated factors keep it engaged with the template.

notes.A: DNA polymerase I has important roles in primer replacement and repair, but performs less of the main fork elongation.
notes.B: DNA polymerase II is more strongly associated with repair and responses to replication stress.
notes.C: RNA polymerase core synthesises RNA during transcription rather than replicating the bacterial chromosome.
notes.D: Terminal transferase adds nucleotides to DNA ends without a template and is not the bacterial replicative enzyme.

questions.stem: Which E. coli DNA polymerase possesses 5-prime to 3-prime exonuclease activity for primer removal?
questions.why: E. coli DNA polymerase I can remove downstream primer material through its 5′ to 3′ exonuclease activity. Its polymerase activity replaces the removed stretch with DNA.

notes.A: DNA polymerase II has proofreading activity, but is not the canonical 5′ to 3′ primer-removing polymerase.
notes.C: DNA polymerase III is the major replicative enzyme and uses a 3′ to 5′ exonuclease for proofreading.
notes.D: RNA polymerase core transcribes genes rather than removing RNA primers from DNA.
notes.E: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase is a template-independent DNA-adding enzyme, not a primer-removing exonuclease.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is primarily responsible for mitochondrial DNA replication in human cells?
questions.why: Human mitochondria use DNA polymerase gamma to copy their genome. The enzyme is distinct from the polymerases that replicate or repair most nuclear DNA.

notes.A: DNA polymerase alpha partners with primase during initiation of nuclear DNA synthesis.
notes.B: DNA polymerase beta is chiefly involved in short-patch nuclear base-excision repair.
notes.C: DNA polymerase delta extends nuclear DNA, especially discontinuous lagging-strand products.
notes.E: DNA polymerase epsilon contributes to nuclear DNA replication rather than being the main mitochondrial polymerase.

questions.stem: Which replication factor acts as a sliding clamp in eukaryotic cells?
questions.why: Proliferating cell nuclear antigen assembles into a ring around duplex DNA. The clamp reduces polymerase dissociation and increases the number of nucleotides added per binding event.

notes.B: Single-stranded DNA-binding proteins protect exposed DNA but do not form the replicative sliding clamp.
notes.C: Ribosomal protein S6 is part of the small ribosomal subunit and does not tether DNA polymerase.
notes.D: Nuclear lamin B forms part of the nuclear lamina rather than encircling replicating DNA.
notes.E: Transcription factor IIB helps initiate RNA polymerase II transcription rather than supporting DNA polymerase processivity.

questions.stem: Why do the ends of linear chromosomes present a replication problem?

options.label: A
options.text: DNA ligase cannot function in nuclei

options.label: B
options.text: Purine nucleotides are absent from telomeres

options.label: C
options.text: Final RNA primer removal leaves an unfilled end

options.label: D
options.text: Helicase cannot bind any eukaryotic DNA

options.label: E
options.text: DNA polymerases initiate synthesis without primers

questions.why: Removal of the outermost lagging-strand RNA primer can leave an unfilled region at the 5′ end. Conventional polymerases lack an upstream 3′ hydroxyl from which to synthesise replacement DNA.

notes.A: DNA ligases work in nuclei, but ligation alone cannot fill a gap left after terminal primer removal.
notes.B: Human telomere repeats contain adenine and guanine, so lack of purines does not explain the end problem.
notes.D: Helicases can unwind eukaryotic DNA. The problem is the lack of a suitable end for polymerase extension.
notes.E: Conventional replicative DNA polymerases require a primer. That dependence is what makes terminal primer removal problematic.

questions.stem: Which enzyme maintains telomere repeats by using an internal RNA template?
questions.why: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase. It uses a sequence in its own RNA as the template for extending the telomeric DNA strand.

notes.A: DNA gyrase alters bacterial DNA supercoiling and does not add eukaryotic telomere repeats.
notes.B: RNA polymerase I produces a precursor of several ribosomal RNAs rather than extending DNA ends.
notes.C: DNA ligase IV joins DNA ends in repair and does not copy an internal RNA template.
notes.D: Ribonuclease H cleaves RNA in an RNA–DNA hybrid, rather than adding DNA repeats.

questions.stem: Which repeated sequence is characteristic of human telomeric DNA?
questions.why: The G-rich strand of a human telomere contains tandem TTAGGG repeats written 5′ to 3′. Its complementary strand carries the corresponding C-rich sequence.

notes.A: TATAAT is associated with the bacterial promoter minus-ten element rather than human telomeres.
notes.C: AUG is an RNA codon and is not the repeated DNA unit at human chromosome ends.
notes.D: CCA is familiar as the mature tRNA acceptor end and does not describe the human telomeric repeat.
notes.E: Alternating G and C can occur elsewhere in DNA but is not the normal human telomere repeat sequence.

questions.stem: What kind of DNA damage is commonly produced by ultraviolet light?
questions.why: Ultraviolet exposure can form covalent links between neighbouring pyrimidines, such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers. These photoproducts can distort DNA and impede normal copying.

notes.A: Gamma-carboxyglutamate is a modified protein residue rather than a common UV lesion in DNA.
notes.B: The relevant lesion links neighbouring nucleotide bases, not peptide chains.
notes.C: A retinal Schiff base links a visual chromophore to opsin and does not describe DNA damage.
notes.E: Allysine-derived bridges cross-link extracellular collagen rather than connecting bases in DNA.

questions.stem: Which pathway principally removes bulky UV-induced photoproducts in human cells?
questions.why: Nucleotide excision repair recognises bulky lesions that distort the duplex. A short DNA segment containing the damaged bases is removed and replaced by synthesis using the intact strand.

notes.B: Mismatch repair corrects base-pairing errors left after replication rather than being the principal route for UV photoproducts.
notes.C: Telomerase adds repeats at chromosome ends and does not excise UV lesions from internal DNA.
notes.D: RNA splicing removes introns from RNA transcripts, not nucleotides from damaged DNA.
notes.E: Translation makes a polypeptide and is not an excision pathway for bulky DNA lesions.

questions.stem: Which disease classically results from inherited defects in nucleotide excision repair of UV damage?
questions.why: In most forms of xeroderma pigmentosum, an inherited defect limits removal of UV-induced DNA damage by nucleotide excision repair. Persistent lesions increase sunlight sensitivity and skin cancer risk.

notes.A: Osteogenesis imperfecta commonly involves type I collagen abnormalities that weaken bone.
notes.B: Lesch–Nyhan syndrome is a purine salvage disorder caused by severe HGPRT deficiency.
notes.D: Hereditary orotic aciduria is a defect in pyrimidine synthesis rather than removal of UV damage.
notes.E: Cystic fibrosis involves defective CFTR-dependent ion transport, not deficient nucleotide excision repair.

questions.stem: Which pathway commonly removes uracil formed by spontaneous cytosine deamination in DNA?
questions.why: Uracil-DNA glycosylase removes uracil from its sugar, leaving an abasic site. Base excision repair then processes the site and restores a correct nucleotide.

notes.A: Telomeric replication maintains chromosome ends rather than removing a deaminated base.
notes.B: Translation terminates at stop codons in mRNA and does not correct lesions in DNA.
notes.C: Ubiquitination attaches ubiquitin to proteins and does not excise uracil from a nucleotide.
notes.D: Fibrin cross-linking stabilises a blood clot and is unrelated to the repair of a DNA base.

questions.stem: Which enzyme first removes a damaged base without initially cutting the complete DNA backbone?
questions.why: A DNA glycosylase hydrolyses the bond between the selected damaged base and its sugar. This leaves an abasic site for later backbone processing.

notes.A: DNA polymerase III carries out bacterial DNA synthesis and does not initiate base excision by removing a base alone.
notes.C: DNA ligase I closes a nick later in DNA processing rather than cutting the base–sugar linkage.
notes.D: Primase makes primers for replication and does not produce abasic sites by removing a damaged base.
notes.E: RNA helicases remodel RNA structures or complexes, rather than excising a base from DNA.

questions.stem: Which proofreading direction removes a wrongly inserted nucleotide during replication?
questions.why: A replicative proofreading exonuclease removes a mismatched nucleotide from the new strand's 3′ end. This 3′ to 5′ removal regenerates the end needed to resume synthesis.

notes.A: The 5′ to 3′ polymerase activity adds nucleotides. Its associated exonuclease performs removal.
notes.B: Replicative synthesis extends 5′ to 3′, while 3′ to 5′ proofreading uses an exonuclease activity.
notes.C: DNA methylases transfer chemical groups and do not correct a mismatched growing terminus by excision.
notes.E: DNA ligase joins adjacent backbone ends rather than removing a misincorporated nucleotide.

questions.stem: Which repair pathway corrects base-pair mismatches that escape replicative proofreading?
questions.why: Mismatch repair detects certain incorrectly paired bases and small insertion or deletion loops left after replication. It replaces a tract of the new strand using the parental strand as a template.

notes.B: Telomeric recombination can help maintain ends in some cells but is not the standard repair route for copying errors.
notes.C: Transcriptional attenuation regulates RNA synthesis and does not remove incorrect bases from DNA.
notes.D: Spliceosomes process RNA rather than correcting mismatched pairs in a newly replicated DNA duplex.
notes.E: Proteolysis acts on proteins. Repair of a replication mismatch requires processing of DNA.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a nonsense mutation from a missense mutation?

options.label: A
options.text: It replaces one amino acid with another

options.label: B
options.text: It leaves the translated protein unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: It generates a premature stop codon

options.label: D
options.text: It removes a whole chromosome arm

options.label: E
options.text: It inserts a new promoter into DNA

questions.why: A nonsense mutation changes a coding triplet into a stop codon. Translation can end early, whereas a missense mutation specifies a different amino acid.

notes.A: Replacement of one amino acid with another is the definition of a missense change.
notes.B: An unchanged amino acid sequence can result from a synonymous substitution, which does not create a premature stop.
notes.D: Loss of a whole chromosome arm is a large structural change rather than a coding triplet becoming a stop.
notes.E: Addition of a promoter might change transcription but does not define a nonsense change in the coding sequence.

questions.stem: Which molecular change is typical of a frameshift mutation?

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of a noncoding telomeric repeat

options.label: E
options.text: An indel not divisible by three

questions.why: An insertion or deletion in a coding sequence shifts the reading frame if its length is not a multiple of three. Codon groupings downstream of the change are then altered.

notes.A: A synonymous substitution affects one base without changing how subsequent bases are grouped into codons.
notes.B: Histone acetylation alters chromatin regulation while leaving the coding sequence length intact.
notes.C: The 5′ cap is an RNA modification and is not part of the translated triplet register.
notes.D: A noncoding telomeric change occurs outside a protein reading frame and does not shift its codon grouping.

questions.stem: Which spontaneous reaction can turn a DNA cytosine into uracil?
questions.why: Hydrolytic deamination replaces a cytosine amino group with a carbonyl, producing uracil. Repair can remove this atypical base before it is copied as a mutation.

notes.A: Gamma-carboxylation adds a carboxyl group to certain protein residues rather than converting a DNA base into uracil.
notes.C: Lysine acetylation modifies a protein side chain, not the exocyclic amino group of cytosine.
notes.D: Cysteine oxidation affects sulphur-containing amino acid residues rather than nitrogenous DNA bases.
notes.E: The amino group being removed belongs to a DNA base rather than to a peptide.
